claims.text: Reliable formation of noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials is achieved when synthesis promotes balanced atomic diffusion and equal constituent mobilities.
Balanced atomic diffusion enhances the catalytic performance of noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials.
Atomic-size mismatch produces local lattice distortions and a rough energy landscape.
The rough energy landscape limits large-scale compositional segregation and defect clustering.
Suppression of segregation and defect clustering ensures a uniform, stable distribution of catalytic active sites.
As-synthesized noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials can form homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions with nanoscale grains.
The initial noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials have minimal compositional segregation.
Changing synthesis or annealing temperature systematically alters constituent-atom diffusion kinetics during nanoparticle formation.
A moderate synthesis-temperature regime avoids excessive phase separation.
Local lattice strain caused by atomic-size mismatch modulates nanoscale diffusion kinetics.
A balanced diffusion environment makes the mobilities of all constituent atoms energetically similar.
Equalized constituent mobility minimizes detrimental defect clusters and compositional segregation.
Continuous defect recombination contributes to a uniform distribution of atoms.
Uniform atomic distributions produce catalytic surfaces with evenly and reliably presented active sites.
A tungsten-based W-Ta-V-Cr HEA shows suppression of irradiation-created dislocation loops.
Noble metal–based HEAs prepared at an optimal temperature will have more uniform active surfaces than samples prepared at higher temperatures.
Noble metal–based HEAs prepared at an optimal temperature will exhibit higher turnover frequency and stability than samples prepared at higher temperatures.
Higher synthesis temperatures cause excessive atomic mobility, phase separation, defect clustering, and less uniform active sites.
The proposed relationship is limited to nanoscale HEAs under moderate-temperature, kinetically controlled synthesis conditions.
Temperatures high enough to trigger thermodynamic phase separation and highly corrosive environments fall outside the hypothesis's expected domain.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field characterizes the as-synthesized material as homogeneous, single-phase, and minimally segregated, while the baseline is also an as-synthesized higher-temperature sample but is defined as markedly phase-separated or defect-clustered. The design does not clarify that the initial-state description applies only to the successful-temperature condition.

The stated conditions restrict synthesis to a moderate regime that does not drive excessive phase separation, but the baseline requires temperatures that cause marked phase separation and therefore appears to lie outside the declared experimental conditions and hypothesis boundary.
